items.title: Creates have no version, and that leaves retries unsafe
items.body:
An expected version protects an edit against content that changed since you loaded it. A create has no earlier version to compare with, so create-post and comment carry none. The comment branch shows it: it checks that comments are not locked and pushes a new comment with a fresh id. If the response is lost and the client sends the comment again, a second comment is created. The guide sums it up: the creates are not stale-safe *and* not retry-safe. The fix is a durable receipt keyed by actor, operation and client request ID, checked inside the same transaction.

- "The version is in the session cookie": the guide says creates have no earlier version at all.
- "Desired-state commands, idempotent like a vote": only vote and follow are desired state; the guide says this does not make comment creation idempotent.
- "BEGIN IMMEDIATE deduplicates": the lock orders writes; it cannot know two comments are the same request.

excerpts.quote: Commands without a version are either desired state (vote, follow: sending `enabled: true` twice is harmless) or create a new record (create post, comment), where there is no earlier version to be stale against.
db.comments.push({ id: uid("comment"),
A useful receipt key includes the authenticated actor, operation, and client request ID.

items.title: Two processes test the real database lock
items.body:
Each worker process runs `tests/worker.ts`, which asks ten times to enable a vote for the same user and idea. Two separate processes cannot share an in-memory queue or variable, so the only thing that can keep them from clashing is the database's own lock. The test then checks that one vote exists and every revision is accounted for, which is a much stronger claim than two calls in a row inside one process.

- "Each process needs its own session secret": both workers use the same demo user; the test is not about cookies.
- "node:test cannot run two async calls": the guide's point is that an in-memory Promise queue cannot coordinate **processes**.
- "Doubles the speed": the goal is real contention, not speed.

excerpts.quote: for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) await executeCommand(demoUsers[0], { action: "vote", postId: "post-keyboard", enabled: true, });
An in-memory Promise queue cannot coordinate those processes, which is why this scenario is stronger than calling the same function twice sequentially in one test process.

items.title: Keep the version check after a table migration
items.body:
Today one document holds everything, and `expected()` checks the version inside one transaction. After moving to relational tables, writes touch separate rows, and it is easy to drop the version check "because the transaction handles it". The guide says that must not happen: the expected-version predicate must stay part of the write.

- "The 16 MiB cap on every table": that cap belongs to the single JSON document; a relational design replaces it with tables and indexes.
- "BEGIN IMMEDIATE around every SELECT": the guide does not ask for this.
- "Cascading deletes from posts to audits": the guide warns the opposite: cascading audit deletes could erase the history the app promises to keep.

excerpts.quote: The expected-version predicate must remain part of the write, not disappear because transactions now update separate rows.
A strict audit foreign key with cascading delete could erase the very history the application promises to preserve.

items.title: Three separate checks: who you are, what you may do, what you may see
items.body:
The concepts guide splits access into three questions.

- **Authentication**: who sent this request? Here a session is a signed, expiring payload. A bare user ID is not a session.
- **Authorization**: may this person do this action? The service reloads the current user inside the write transaction, so an object that merely looks like an admin cannot grant admin rights.
- **Visibility**: may this person even see this record? Customers cannot read internal ideas, and hidden ideas vanish from public views.

The key habit: the **service** enforces all three, not the page. A hidden button is nice presentation, but a client can call a server action without clicking anything. When you read a command branch in `service.ts`, look for the `insist(...)` lines at the top: each one is a rule that must hold before anything is written.

excerpts.quote: Authentication answers who supplied a valid session.
Authorization answers whether the current identity may perform a particular action.
Hiding a button is helpful presentation, but a client can call a server action without clicking that button. The service must enforce the rule independently.

readMore.why: How a session payload is signed and given an expiry.

items.title: transact refuses async callbacks
items.body:
`transact` calls the change function and then, before committing, checks `result instanceof Promise`. An `async` function always returns a Promise, so the check throws "Transactions must be synchronous", and the `catch` rolls back. Without this check, the async work would finish *after* `COMMIT`, changing a document copy that is no longer being saved, so those changes would be silently lost.

- "TypeScript rejects async callbacks at compile time": then no runtime check would be needed; the guide says the explicit check is what prevents the bug.
- "Commits and runs the async part in the background": that is the bug itself, not a safe design.
- "Awaits the Promise before committing": `transact` is synchronous; it throws instead of awaiting.

excerpts.quote: const result = change(current); if (result instanceof Promise) throw new Error("Transactions must be synchronous");
an `async` callback would return a Promise that resolves after `COMMIT`, which is exactly the bug the explicit `instanceof Promise` check prevents.

items.title: Serialized writes still let stale edits through
items.body:
BEGIN IMMEDIATE makes writes take turns. It does not know what each user *saw*. Alice and Bob both loaded version 3 before either transaction started. Alice saves; the post becomes version 4. Bob's transaction runs next, on its turn, and would happily overwrite Alice's text. Only comparing Bob's expected version 3 with the current 4 catches this lost update. The guide says serializing writes alone would not detect it.

- "SQLite merges titles character by character": nothing merges; one write replaces the other.
- "BEGIN IMMEDIATE only works within one process": the guide says it stops two **processes** both reading then writing.
- "Not needed, it counts edits": the version exists to reject stale saves with 409.

excerpts.quote: Alice and Bob can both read version 3 before either starts a transaction. Alice saves version 3 and creates version 4. Bob's later transaction must reject his expected version 3. Serializing database writes alone would not detect that Bob edited stale content.

items.title: Start here: a feedback board that many people edit at once
items.body:
The product is a small feedback board: customers post ideas, vote, follow and comment; moderators and product managers merge, hide and change status. The engineering lesson is what keeps it correct when several people change related records at the same time.

Read in the course's order:

1. `astraupskill/README.md` - the study sequence and what you should be able to explain.
2. `01-CODEBASE-MAP.md` - trace one vote from its button to the saved database document.
3. `02-CONCEPTS.md` - read it twice if transactions are new to you. Most quizzes come from here.
4. `03-WORKED-CHANGE.md` - a stale edit in two browser tabs.
5. `04-TESTING-AND-DEBUGGING.md` - how each test proves one promise.
6. `05-PRACTICE.md`, then `06-SOLUTIONS-AND-REVIEW.md` only after trying the tasks.

Keep `src/server/store.ts` and `src/modules/feedback/service.ts` open; the guides quote them by line number.

excerpts.quote: If you have never seen a database transaction, read `02-CONCEPTS.md` twice rather than once; everything else rests on it.
trace one vote from its button to the committed database document.

readMore.why: Where each layer lives, from page to service to store.
A step-by-step stale-edit scenario using two browser tabs.

items.title: Merge refuses a source that others already point at
items.body:
Before `merge` marks the source as a duplicate, it runs a list of `insist` checks. One of them asks: does any post already have `duplicateOfPostId === source.id`? Here C points at A, so the answer is yes, and the merge fails with status 409 and the message "This source is already a canonical target; merge its duplicates separately first." The concepts guide says preventing duplicate chains keeps the merge relationship understandable.

- "C is silently re-pointed to B": the code throws before any change; nothing re-points C.
- "400, sources must have no votes": a merge **moves** votes and follows to the target; votes do not block it.
- "C points at A which points at B": that chain is exactly what the check prevents.

excerpts.quote: insist( !db.posts.some((x) => x.duplicateOfPostId === source.id), 409, "This source is already a canonical target; merge its duplicates separately first.", );
Matching visibility and preventing duplicate chains keep that relationship understandable.

items.title: enabled: true twice leaves one vote
items.body:
A vote command says what the final state should be, not "flip it". The service first checks whether this user already has a vote on this post. It pushes a new vote only when `cmd.enabled && !exists`. The second identical request finds the vote already there and does nothing. The guide calls this desired state plus a unique user/post pair.

- "Two votes, no unique check": the `exists` check is exactly that uniqueness check.
- "Zero votes, it toggles": only `enabled: false` removes a vote; the command is not a toggle.
- "409, votes carry a version": vote and follow have no expected version; they are desired state.

excerpts.quote: if (cmd.enabled && !exists)
A command saying `enabled: true` is naturally repeatable. Sending it twice should leave one vote.

items.title: Re-read the record after a rejection
items.body:
The test saves once with version 1 (accepted), then tries again with the same old version. `assert.rejects` proves the second call threw. But a command could have changed data **before** it threw. So the last line re-reads the post and checks the first title is still stored. The guide calls missing writes-before-the-error the most common way a "conflict is handled" claim turns out false.

- "The first save might have been rejected": `await run(cmd)` would throw and fail the test if so; the first save is the accepted baseline.
- "assert.rejects is flaky": the guide makes no such claim; it is about what the assertion cannot see.
- "The message text may change": that is about the regex, not why a second assertion is needed.

excerpts.quote: await run(cmd); await assert.rejects(run({ ...cmd, title: "Stale title" }), /record changed/); assert.equal(post().title, "First accepted title");
Merely asserting an error misses accidental writes performed before the error was thrown

items.title: A version check is real only inside the transaction
items.body:
The page keeps the version it loaded and sends it as `cmd.version`. In `editPost` the service calls `expected(p, cmd.version)`, where `p` is the record **as it exists inside the transaction right now**. If someone saved in between, the numbers differ and the save fails with 409. Only after every guard passes does `touch(p)` bump the version. The guide calls this the difference between checking a version and merely displaying one.

- "Compares with the session cookie": the cookie holds the session, not post versions.
- "Re-fetches the current version just before saving": that would always match, turning a stale overwrite into an apparently valid save; the guide warns against it.
- "Runs in the client form": the check is in the server's service, on the stored record.

excerpts.quote: `expected` runs *inside* the transaction, on the record as it exists at that moment --- not on the copy the page rendered.
touch(p); // version++ and timestamps, only after every guard passed
Avoid silently rewriting a stale version to the current one. That would convert an unreviewed overwrite into an apparently valid save.

items.title: The storage choice: one validated JSON document in SQLite
items.body:
This board stores the **whole workspace** as one JSON document in a single SQLite row. Every command reads that document, changes it in memory, validates all of it and writes it back as one unit.

Why do it this way? It makes transactions simple and the data easy to inspect: there is only one thing to lock and one thing to write. The cost is that every write serializes the whole workspace, so the guide caps collections and document size and says clearly that this is for a small local board, not unlimited scale.

Keep this picture in mind when you read the store: one read, one change function, one validation, one write. Later the course asks what must survive if the data moves into real relational tables; the answer is "the same business rules", stated before any infrastructure change.

excerpts.quote: A single validated JSON aggregate inside SQLite is easy to transact and inspect, but every write validates and serializes the whole workspace.
This is suitable for studying a small local board, not a claim of unlimited scale.

readMore.why: The store: how the document is opened, decoded, validated and written.

items.title: An idea with a vote cannot be deleted
items.body:
`deletePost` is strict. It requires the author, the expected version and status Open. Then it checks whether anything references the post: votes, follows, comments, flags, official updates, internal notes or merge history. One vote is a reference, so the command fails with 409 and the message "This idea has discussion or history. Hide it instead of deleting it." The concepts guide gives the reason: once an idea has support or discussion, hiding is the right workflow.

- "403, only moderators may delete": the rule is the opposite; only the **author** may delete an unused idea.
- "Deleted and the vote reassigned": nothing moves votes on delete; only merge moves them.
- "Deleted with its vote": the reference check refuses before anything is removed.

excerpts.quote: insist( !referenced, 409, "This idea has discussion or history. Hide it instead of deleting it.", );
Once it has discussion, support, or moderation references, deletion is rejected and hiding becomes the appropriate workflow.

items.title: An empty list does not say why it is empty
items.body:
The service already tells the page *why* there may be no posts: it returns `guestBlocked`, which is true when there is no user and guest browsing is off. So the page decides in order: if `guestBlocked`, say "sign in"; otherwise, if a search or status filter is active, say "no matches, clear your filters"; otherwise, "nothing here yet". The guide warns not to read permission from `posts.length === 0`, because a signed-in user can simply have no matches.

- "Check whether categories is empty": categories are a separate field; the blocked state has its own flag.
- "Always show 'nothing here yet'": that hides both the sign-in case and the filter case.
- "Show 'sign in' whenever the list is empty": this is the exact inference the guide forbids.

excerpts.quote: guestBlocked: !u && !db.settings.allowGuestBrowsing,
`guestBlocked` means "sign in", an empty list with a query or status filter means "no matches, clear your filters", and an empty list with no filters means "nothing here yet, be the first".
Do not infer permission from `posts.length === 0`, because an authenticated user can legitimately have no matches.

items.title: BEGIN IMMEDIATE locks before reading
items.body:
A plain `BEGIN` in SQLite takes its write lock later, when the first write happens. Two processes could then both read the same document, both change it, and one save would wipe out the other. `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` takes the write lock **first**, before the `SELECT`, so the second process waits until the first has committed and then reads the new document.

- "Plain BEGIN is not supported": the guide gives the lock timing as the reason, not missing support.
- "IMMEDIATE commits each statement": the code commits once, with an explicit `COMMIT` at the end.
- "IMMEDIATE is read-only until UPDATE": it is the opposite; it takes the write lock at the start.

excerpts.quote: db.exec("BEGIN IMMEDIATE"); const row = db.prepare("SELECT document FROM workspace WHERE id=1").get();
`BEGIN IMMEDIATE` takes the write lock *before* reading, so two processes cannot both read the same document and then both write.
